name: Chikunda
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Guérois, Rozenn. 2025. Quem disse que Chikunda não era língua? Estudo (socio-)linguístico preliminar de uma língua Bantu transfronteiriça minoritária. Revista Científica da Universidade Eduardo Mondlane, Série: Letras e Ciências Sociais 5(2): 197-226. DOI 10.70778/rhbgzj49 (CC BY 4.0; publisher PDF).
catalog_locator: Section 'Fonologia' > 'Tonologia', pp. 210-211; the accent statement is the last paragraph of p. 211. Supporting: p. 209 vowels/length; p. 212 'prosódia semi-tonal/semi-acentual'; p. 217 verbal tone patterns; endnote vi (phonological phrasing).
catalog_quote: [p. 210] Conforme à maioria das línguas bantu, mas de forma inesperada na zona N40, o Chikunda tem tons fonêmicos. No entanto, o sistema tonal chikunda aparece bastante erodido, com uns contrastes tonais principalmente visíveis no domínio lexical. ... [p. 211] Fora do léxico, o sistema tonal do Chikunda parece bastante enfraquecido, sugerindo um processo de simplificação e reanálise tonal que tem levado ao surgimento de um acento demarcativo na penúltima UPT da frase fonológica. Isso pode significar que, embora os tons tenham sido originalmente contrastivos na gramática, eles foram gradualmente perdidos ou neutralizados em unidades prosódicas maiores, resultando em um sistema de acento semelhante ao estresse (como em Suaíli e outras línguas da zona N), que marca os limites da frase em vez de preservar os contrastes tonais lexicais. ... [p. 217] Na grande maioria dos casos, um único tom alto ancora-se na penúltima UPT, de forma semelhante a um sistema acentual.

new_statements.translation: Outside the lexicon, the Chikunda tone system appears rather weakened, suggesting a process of tonal simplification and reanalysis that has led to the emergence of a demarcative accent on the penultimate TBU [tone-bearing unit] of the phonological phrase. This may mean that, although tones were originally contrastive in the grammar, they were gradually lost or neutralised in larger prosodic units, resulting in a stress-like accent system (as in Swahili and other zone-N languages) which marks phrase boundaries rather than preserving lexical tonal contrasts.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Chikunda is a tone language (privative H vs Ø, with H doubling onto the following TBU and final lowering), but the tone system is eroded: outside the lexicon a demarcative accent falls on the penultimate tone-bearing unit (vowel) of the phonological phrase, a stress-like penultimate accent of the Swahili/zone-N type. In isolation words cannot end in H, so H-final patterns surface as HØ; lexical H doubled onto the penult is realised falling. Vowel length is not phonemic (used only expressively), so the penultimate prominence is not described as penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: The author calls the analysis preliminary and non-exhaustive; she leaves open whether the penultimate accent is fully predictable or whether some lexical tones resist neutralisation ('É preciso mais dados experimentais para testar se a acentuação penúltima é totalmente previsível ou se há casos em que certos tons lexicais resistem à neutralização', p. 211), and offers an alternative analysis as phrase-level tone-shift rules. Lexically, HØ vs ØØ patterns exist in disyllabic stems and ØHØ/HØØ etc. in longer stems (Tables 3-4, pp. 210-211); bare infinitives anchor H on the first TBU of the stem (p. 211).
new_statements.domain_note: The accent is stated for the phonological phrase (connected speech), not the isolated word; isolated words show lexical H tones with final lowering. Data from recent fieldwork in Zambia, Mozambique and Zimbabwe; the southern-Malawi variety is excluded (p. 203).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kund1255 'Chikunda' (ISO kdn; point -15.73, 30.28 at the Luangwa–Zambezi confluence) is the Zambezi-valley Chikunda of Zumbo (MZ), Luangwa/Feira (ZM), Kanyemba (ZW) and southern Malawi — exactly the variety Guérois 2025 describes (fieldwork in ZM/MZ/ZW; Malawi variety excluded). The 'Kunda' of Mambwe district, Eastern Province, Zambia (Zemba 2015; Banda et al. 2013; the 'Kunda' of Kashoki & Mann 1978) is a different language: Guérois 2025: 199-200 states that Guthrie's N42 and Zemba conflated the two by name, and that the Mambwe Kunda is classified as a variant of Nsenga N41 (nsen1242) per Hammarström 2019. Ethnologue/ISO kdn lumps both; the catalog entry for kund1255 should rest on Guérois 2025 only, and Zemba 2015 belongs (if anywhere) with nsen1242.

sources.note: Section 'Fonologia > Tonologia' (pp. 209-212): Chikunda has phonemic tone (H vs Ø) but an eroded system; H tones double onto the next TBU except phrase-finally; outside the lexicon the tone system is weak, 'suggesting.. the emergence of a demarcative accent on the penultimate TBU of the phonological phrase', i.e. a stress-like system as in Swahili and other zone-N languages; vowel length not phonemic (p. 209); author flags the analysis as preliminary and asks for experimental data on whether penultimate accentuation is fully predictable (p. 211).

sources.citation: Zemba, Mercy. 2015. A grammatical sketch of Kunda language. MA dissertation, University of Zambia, Lusaka. 162 pp.
sources.note: Chapter 4 Phonology (pp. 23-31) has nothing on stress or accent; vowel length 'distinctive.. though not phonemically contrastive', no penultimate-lengthening rule stated (p. 24); 4.2 Tone (p. 30): 'limited use of tone.. no lexical nor grammatical minimal pairs.. this study will not deal with tone'; 3.1.6: 'The study has not included tone.' NB describes the Kunda of Mambwe district, Eastern Province, Zambia (chiefdoms Nsefu, Mnkhanya, Jumbe) — per Guérois 2025: 199-200 a different language (a variant of Nsenga N41), conflated with Chikunda by Guthrie's N42 and by ISO kdn.
